      Theory & explanations

      What is galvanic corrosion?

      Galvanic (bimetallic, dissimilar-metal) corrosion is the accelerated corrosion of one metal caused by electrical contact with a more noble metal or conductor in a common electrolyte. The couple forms an electrochemical cell: the less noble metal becomes the anode and its oxidation (M → Mn+ + ne−) speeds up, while the more noble metal becomes the cathode, where oxygen reduction (O2 + 2H2O + 4e− → 4OH−) or hydrogen evolution takes place and its own corrosion slows down (Fontana, 1986; Jones, 1996).

      Three conditions must all be met, and removing any one of them stops the cell:

      1. two materials with different corrosion potentials,
      2. an electrical (metallic) path between them,
      3. a continuous electrolyte (seawater, condensation, wet deposits) wetting both.

      Galvanic series, not the EMF series

      The standard electrode potentials (EMF series) apply to pure metals in solutions of their own ions at unit activity, and rank aluminium and titanium as very active. In practice their passive oxide films shift them far in the noble direction. A galvanic series instead lists measured corrosion potentials of real alloys in a specific environment. ASTM G82 explains how such a series is built and stresses that it is only valid for the environment in which it was measured. This tool uses the classic series in flowing seawater (LaQue, 1975), which is the most widely published and is a conservative reference for other aqueous environments.

      Stainless steels appear twice: passive (aerated, free surfaces) and active (inside crevices, under deposits or in stagnant, oxygen-depleted water). The same alloy can change sides in a couple depending on where it is.

      Potential difference and the risk limit

      The driving force of the cell is the potential difference between the two members:

      ΔE = Ecorr, cathode − Ecorr, anode

      Design guidance derived from the anodic index (MIL-STD-889 practice and earlier MIL-F-14072) limits ΔE to about 0.15 V in harsh environments (marine, salt spray, high humidity), 0.25 V in normal environments and 0.50 V in controlled, dry environments. This tool shows ΔE from the mid-range values and the band from the range extremes, and grades the risk against these limits.

      Why ΔE alone is not the whole story: mixed-potential theory

      According to mixed-potential theory (Wagner & Traud, 1938), the coupled metals polarise to a common galvanic potential Eg at which the total anodic current equals the total cathodic current. The galvanic current, and so the corrosion rate, depends on the polarisation behaviour (kinetics) of both electrodes and on the electrolyte resistance, not only on ΔE (Zhang, 2011; Revie & Uhlig, 2008). Consequences:

      • A noble metal on which oxygen reduction is slow (e.g. titanium, passive stainless) can be a weaker cathode than its potential suggests; copper alloys and graphite are efficient cathodes.
      • A highly polarisable, passive anode such as titanium barely corrodes even when it is the more negative member.
      • In low-conductivity water (fresh water, thin condensate films) the attack is limited to a narrow zone near the junction; in seawater it spreads further.

      Area ratio effect

      Charge conservation requires Ia = Ic. If the cathodic reaction is limited by oxygen supply to the cathode surface, the galvanic current is roughly proportional to the cathode area, so the anodic current density is

      ia ≈ ic · Ac / Aa

      A small anode next to a large cathode (steel rivets in copper plate) corrodes very quickly; a large anode with a small cathode (stainless bolts in an aluminium plate) suffers only mild, spread-out attack (Fontana, 1986; Francis, 2001). For the same reason, painting only the anode is dangerous: every coating defect becomes a tiny anode facing the whole cathode.

      Other factors

      • Electrolyte: chlorides, conductivity, temperature and flow velocity all raise the galvanic current. Seawater and de-icing salts are the most severe.
      • Time of wetness: atmospheric galvanic corrosion only runs while a moisture film is present (ISO 9223 corrosivity categories C1–CX).
      • Distance: the attack is concentrated next to the contact line.
      • Corrosion products can stifle or reverse the couple over time (e.g. zinc and steel in hot water above about 60 °C).

      Prevention

      • Select materials close together in the galvanic series; make fasteners and other small parts slightly more noble than the structure.
      • Insulate: non-conductive washers, sleeves and gaskets, with no bypass through bolts or brackets.
      • Exclude the electrolyte: sealants, jointing compounds, wet installation of fasteners, drainage.
      • Coat the cathode (or both members), not only the anode.
      • Apply cathodic protection with sacrificial anodes or impressed current in immersion service.

      The galvanic series ranks risk; it does not predict corrosion rates. For critical designs measure the couple in the real electrolyte (ASTM G71) or consult a corrosion engineer.

      4. MIL-STD-889. Dissimilar Metals (galvanic compatibility of electrically conductive materials). U.S. Department of Defense. Compatibility practice and anodic-index limits.
      5. Wagner, C., & Traud, W. (1938). Über die Deutung von Korrosionsvorgängen durch Überlagerung von elektrochemischen Teilvorgängen und über die Potentialbildung an Mischelektroden. Zeitschrift für Elektrochemie, 44, 391–402. Mixed-potential theory.
      6. Fontana, M. G. (1986). Corrosion Engineering (3rd ed.). McGraw-Hill, New York. Ch. 3, Galvanic or two-metal corrosion. Area effect, distance effect, prevention.
      7. Jones, D. A. (1996). Principles and Prevention of Corrosion (2nd ed.). Prentice Hall, Upper Saddle River, NJ. Ch. 6, Galvanic and concentration cell corrosion. Electrochemistry and polarisation of couples.
      8. Revie, R. W., & Uhlig, H. H. (2008). Corrosion and Corrosion Control: An Introduction to Corrosion Science and Engineering (4th ed.). Wiley, Hoboken, NJ. EMF series versus galvanic series, passivity.

      11. Hack, H. P. (Ed.) (1988). Galvanic Corrosion. ASTM STP 978. ASTM, Philadelphia. Collected research papers on galvanic corrosion.

      Galvanic Corrosion Checker

      Version 1.0 · by Eren Tozlu

      A free, browser-based tool to check the galvanic corrosion risk of two materials in contact. Pick the materials and the environment: it shows the potential difference in the seawater galvanic series, which material corrodes, and a colour-coded risk with the effect of the area ratio, plus recommendations. All calculations run in your browser.

      Potentials follow the galvanic series of ASTM G82 (after LaQue); the environment limits follow the anodic-index guidance used with MIL-STD-889. The Theory section and the reference list explain the method.

      Made by Eren Tozlu. More engineering tools and projects at ehcrea.com.

      How to use the Galvanic Corrosion Checker

      New here? Pick an example from Load application example… in the toolbar, then change one input at a time.

      Three steps

      1. Material couple: choose the two materials that touch. For plated parts choose the plating metal. ⇅ swaps them.
      2. Environment: Harsh for marine, immersion, salt spray or de-icing salts; Normal for outdoor and unconditioned indoor spaces; Controlled for dry, air-conditioned spaces. Then the area ratio of the cathode (more noble metal) to the anode.
      3. Read the result: ΔE, which material corrodes, and the colour of the risk indicator.

      Risk levels

      Low
      ΔE within the limit for the environment. Compatible.
      Moderate
      Up to the next step of the 0.15 / 0.25 / 0.50 / 0.75 / 1.00 V ladder. Seal or isolate the joint.
      High
      Two steps above the limit. Avoid, or isolate and keep water out.
      Severe
      More than that. Change a material or fully isolate.

      The area ratio moves the level one step up (small anode, large cathode) or down (large anode, small cathode). If the more negative member is a very stable passive material (titanium, alloy C-276, platinum, graphite) it does not corrode itself, so the level is Low; it can still attack other metals.

      Tips

      • Click a bar in the galvanic series chart to pick material B, Shift-click to pick A.
      • The compatibility matrix shows every pair for the current environment and area ratio; click a cell to load it.
      • Copy link stores the couple and environment in a link.

      The galvanic series ranks risk but does not give corrosion rates. Confirm critical joints by testing.
